label: Open Finance Strategy & Governance
description: Strategy and governance for the move beyond open banking to open finance. Frames the 2023 EU package — PSD3, PSR and FIDA — as PROPOSALS not yet in force, against the in-force PSD2 (EU) 2015/2366. Covers consent-driven data sharing, the data-holder / data-user ecosystem, premium and contractual API schemes, perimeter and authorisation, customer-permission dashboards, liability and fraud-data sharing, and the strategic and product response (monetisation, partnerships, build-vs-buy).

claudeKnowledge.description: In force: PSD2 Directive (EU) 2015/2366; EMD2 Directive 2009/110/EC; GDPR (EU) 2016/679; Data Act (EU) 2023/2854; EBA RTS on SCA & CSC (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389). PROPOSALS (not yet in force, 2023 package): PSD3 (revised payment services directive) COM(2023) 366, PSR (payment services regulation) COM(2023) 367, and FIDA — Financial Data Access framework — COM(2023) 360. Track trilogue / final-text status before relying on article numbers.

guidedInputs.label: Primary role in the open-finance ecosystem
guidedInputs.description: Which role best describes the institution's strategic position? FIDA splits the market into data holders and data users; the same firm can be both.

options.label: Incumbent bank / credit institution (data holder + potential data user)
Insurer / pension provider (in FIDA scope as data holder)
Fintech / third-party provider (primarily a data user)
Aggregator / platform / FISP (financial information service provider)

guidedInputs.label: Jurisdiction(s)
guidedInputs.description: Which markets is the strategy for? FIDA, PSD3 and PSR are EU instruments; passporting and national gold-plating shape the strategy.

guidedInputs.label: Data categories in scope
guidedInputs.description: Which FIDA-eligible data categories beyond payment accounts is the strategy considering? This drives the data-sharing scheme(s) the firm must join or build.

guidedInputs.label: Strategic posture
guidedInputs.description: What stance is the board leaning toward for open finance? Drives the build-vs-buy and monetisation analysis.

options.label: Not yet determined — help frame the choice
Defensive — comply, protect the customer base, minimise leakage
Platform play — become a data hub / aggregator for others
Data-user growth — build new products on others' data
Monetiser — premium / contractual APIs beyond the mandated baseline

guidedInputs.label: Focus areas
guidedInputs.description: Which dimensions of the open-finance strategy should the analysis prioritise?

options.label: Financial-data-sharing schemes & API standards (mandated vs premium)

guidedInputs.label: Known constraints, ambitions or concerns
guidedInputs.description: Describe the firm's current open-banking estate, commercial ambitions, board appetite, and any known constraints or worries.

exampleInput: We are a mid-sized Nordic universal bank (Sweden + Finland, ~3,500 staff) and the board has asked Strategy & Digital for a position paper on open finance before the FIDA trilogue concludes. Today we run Berlin Group PSD2 APIs (live since 2020) purely as a compliance cost centre — AISP/PISP access is free, unmonitored, and we have no premium tier. Beyond payment accounts we hold savings, mortgages, a sizeable investment book and an occupational-pension arm, all of which fall into FIDA's data-holder scope. We're worried about three things: (1) becoming a 'dumb pipe' if fintechs and the big platforms harvest our data while we capture none of the value; (2) what FIDA's mandatory financial-data-sharing schemes and 'reasonable compensation' actually require of us as a data holder versus what we can charge for via premium/contractual APIs; and (3) whether we should be a platform/aggregator ourselves (a data hub for smaller Nordic institutions) or focus on becoming a data user to enrich our own lending and advice. Please frame PSD3, PSR and FIDA correctly as proposals not yet in force, set out the data-holder/data-user ecosystem choices, the perimeter and FISP-authorisation implications, the consent-dashboard and liability/fraud-data-sharing obligations, and give the board a clear build-vs-buy and monetisation decision frame. Known weak spots: no customer-facing permission dashboard today (consents are scattered across product silos), and our legacy core makes real-time non-payment data access genuinely hard.

exampleValues.known_concerns: Berlin Group PSD2 APIs live since 2020 but run as a pure compliance cost centre — free AISP/PISP access, no premium tier, no usage analytics. Board fears 'dumb pipe' outcome. No customer-facing consent dashboard; permissions scattered across product silos. Legacy core makes real-time non-payment data access hard. Occupational-pension arm and investment book bring large new data-holder obligations under FIDA.
